opus-5.5.text:
I think there's enormous value in it, and honestly it's been one of the most important parts of how we've built the team.

When you come into drug design from a pure machine learning background, you don't carry the same assumptions about what's possible or what's "supposed" to be hard. The field has decades of accumulated wisdom, which is incredibly valuable, but it also comes with a lot of implicit constraints: this is how you do structure-based design, this is the order in which you run the assays, this problem is basically unsolvable computationally. Someone who's spent their career training large models on games or language or vision just looks at it differently. They ask, "Okay, what's the data, what's the objective, what's the feedback loop, and how do we scale it?" That framing can unlock approaches that wouldn't naturally emerge from inside the domain.

There's also a real transferable skill set. Building systems that learn from huge amounts of data, designing evaluations that actually tell you whether you're making progress, knowing how to get a model to generalize rather than memorize. Those problems look remarkably similar whether you're predicting the next move in a game or the next conformation of a protein-ligand complex. A lot of the hard-won engineering intuition carries over almost directly.

That said, it only works if you pair those people very closely with deep domain experts: chemists, biologists, people who've actually taken molecules into the clinic. The magic happens in the interaction. The ML researcher asks the naive question that turns out to be profound, and the chemist explains why some seemingly elegant idea would fall apart in a real biological system. You need both. If you only had ML people, you'd build beautiful models that solve the wrong problem. If you only had domain experts, you might not push the methods as far as they can go.

So for us it's less about hiring people without biology knowledge per se, and more about bringing together people with genuinely different ways of thinking, and creating a culture where they learn from each other really quickly. The ML researchers who join tend to pick up the chemistry surprisingly fast, because they're motivated: they can see that the problem is real and that the impact, if you get it right, is huge.

r001.rationale: The response says newcomers ask basic questions about the data, objective, and feedback loop, which can unlock approaches that would not naturally emerge from within the field.

r002.rationale: It describes ML researchers without domain experience as bringing a different perspective that challenges implicit constraints and assumptions in drug design.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's something we've thought about a lot at Isomorphic, and honestly it's a bit counterintuitive to a lot of people in pharma. The way I think about it is that the biggest wins we've seen in this space, going back to AlphaFold, came from people who approached the problem fundamentally as a machine learning problem. They weren't constrained by decades of accumulated intuition about how protein structure prediction "should" be done. They looked at the data, they looked at the structure of the problem, and they built models that could learn the right inductive biases rather than having them hand-coded in.

So when we hire ML researchers who don't have a chemistry or biology background, what we're getting is people who are really, really good at the craft of building models that learn from data at scale, and who don't come in with preconceptions about which features matter or what the right representation of a molecule is. They're willing to ask naive questions, and quite often those naive questions turn out to be exactly the right ones, because the field has sometimes converged on assumptions that were driven by what was tractable twenty years ago rather than what's actually true.

The flip side is that you absolutely need deep domain expertise in the room too. We're not trying to replace medicinal chemists or structural biologists. The magic happens when you put those people side by side with the ML researchers and you create a culture where neither side is in service of the other. The chemists keep us honest about what actually matters for a drug, things like selectivity, ADME properties, the realities of synthesis, and the ML people push back and say, well, why do we believe that, can we test it, can we let the model learn it instead. That friction is really productive.

And the other thing I'd say is that the ML researchers pick up the domain knowledge surprisingly fast when they're embedded in it. Within six months to a year they've got a working understanding of the biology that's good enough to have real conversations. It's much harder to go the other way and teach someone to be a world-class ML researcher in that time. So from a talent perspective, it makes sense to hire for the thing that's rarer and harder to acquire, and then surround those people with the right expertise and the right problems.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers without preconceptions look at the data and structure of the problem, and that their naive questions can expose better approaches. This conveys approaching the problem from first principles.

r002.rationale: The response identifies lack of chemistry or biology background as an advantage: researchers bring fewer preconceptions and can challenge assumptions the field has settled on.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in it, provided you bring them into a team with deep chemistry and biology expertise. A machine learning researcher can look at a problem with fresh eyes and ask, “Why are we framing it this way? Could we learn this from data? Could we design a different experiment?” Sometimes that opens up approaches that wouldn’t otherwise be obvious.

But it has to be a partnership. In drug discovery, you need to understand what your data actually measures, what the limitations are, and whether improving a prediction will help you make a better molecule. That’s where the interaction with chemists and biologists is essential.

So I wouldn’t make prior domain knowledge a prerequisite. I’d look for excellent researchers who are curious, willing to learn, and comfortable having their assumptions challenged. You want them to bring new ideas while developing enough understanding to work on the questions that really matter.

r001.rationale: The response describes asking why a problem is framed a certain way and exploring alternatives, but does not clearly say this enables an approach from first principles.

r002.rationale: It says prior domain knowledge should not be a prerequisite and that fresh eyes can challenge assumptions and reveal new approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of value in it. If you come from machine learning, you might look at a problem differently. You’re asking: What can we learn from the data? How do we represent this problem? Can we build a model that helps us make better decisions? And sometimes that leads you to question assumptions that someone steeped in the field might take for granted.

But you need a close partnership with chemists and biologists. They understand what makes an experiment meaningful, where the data can mislead you, and what constraints actually matter. The opportunity is to bring those perspectives together. You don’t need every machine learning researcher to arrive as an expert in drug discovery, but you do need them to be curious, willing to learn, and able to work deeply with people who are.

r001.rationale: The response describes looking at the problem differently and asking what can be learned from data, but does not clearly connect basic questions to approaching drug-design problems from first principles.

r002.rationale: It says that a machine learning researcher can question assumptions that someone steeped in the field might take for granted, identifying an advantage of coming from outside the field.
